title: Agents, tools and protocols
summary: Build agents from raw API calls up: tool calling on the wire, a bounded loop, context and memory, durable execution, MCP (2026-07-28 stateless spec) with OAuth, Agent Skills, A2A, subagents, coding and browser agents, runtime security, and an eval + observability stack. Frameworks are studied as examples after you can build without them. Primary spine: rohitg00 phases 13–14 + Anthropic engineering posts + official specs.

units.title: Workflows vs agents: when not to build an agent
outcomes: You can classify a task as single call, prompt chain, router, parallelization, orchestrator-workers, evaluator-optimizer or autonomous agent and justify the choice.
You can name the latency/cost/reliability metric that would show an agent is worse than a fixed workflow.

learn.title: Building effective agents
learn.slice: Whole post incl. Appendix 1 (Agents in practice) and Appendix 2 (Prompt engineering your tools)

covers: Definition: workflows (predefined code paths) vs agents (LLM dynamically directs its own process and tool use)

When to use agents and the advice to start with direct LLM API calls before frameworks

practice.title: Five-task architecture triage
practice.brief: Take 5 tasks: FAQ answer, ticket routing, invoice extraction, multi-file code fix, open-ended research. For each pick single call / chain / router / parallel / orchestrator-workers / evaluator-optimizer / agent and justify it in 2 lines with expected latency, cost per task and the failure you fear most. Implement the router one in plain Python against a free model (Ollama or a provider free tier).
practice.done_when: A table of 5 rows (task, pattern, latency estimate, cost estimate, main risk) is committed, and the router runs on 20 sample tickets with ≥ 90% correct routes logged.

options: it uses more than one LLM call
the LLM dynamically directs its own process and tool use
quiz.explain: Workflows follow predefined code paths; agents let the model decide the next step and tool.

quiz.prompt: Best fit for 'classify the support query, then send it to a specialized prompt':
quiz.explain: Routing classifies an input and directs it to a specialised follow-up.

quiz.prompt: The post's recommended first step before adopting a framework is to…
options: use LLM APIs directly and understand the underlying calls
quiz.explain: Frameworks hide prompts and responses; start with a few lines of direct API code.

quiz.prompt: Give one task where an agent is worse than a fixed workflow, and name the metric that would show it.

practice.title: Same tools, two providers, raw JSON
practice.brief: Call two different providers (or one provider plus local Ollama) with the same 3 tools using raw HTTP or the thin SDK, no agent framework. Log the exact request and response JSON, including one turn with two parallel tool calls and one streamed tool call. Validate every argument with Pydantic and feed a validation error back to the model once. Write a 1-page diff of the message formats.
practice.done_when: Repo contains logs/*.json for both providers, a passing pytest that rejects a malformed argument, and a DIFF.md comparing at least 6 fields (tool definition, call id, arguments encoding, result message role, parallel flag, stop reason).

quiz.prompt: A model's tool call is…
options: executed by the provider on your machine
a structured request that your code must validate and execute
a final answer to the user
quiz.explain: The model only proposes; the host executes, so validation and authorization live in your code.

quiz.prompt: Two independent tool calls come back in one turn. You should…
options: run them concurrently and return each result with its matching call id
merge them into one string without ids
quiz.explain: Results must be correlated by id; order of completion can differ from order of request.

quiz.prompt: The main reason to validate tool arguments with a schema/Pydantic is that…
options: models can emit malformed or out-of-range arguments
quiz.explain: Even with constrained decoding, values can be semantically invalid; validate before executing.

practice.title: agent.py — a bounded loop
practice.brief: Build agent.py (~200 lines, no framework): tool registry, loop with max_steps + wall-clock + token budget, a dataclass for state, a StopReason enum, JSONL trace output. Tools: read_file, search_notes, calculator. Then inject a failing tool (raises 50% of the time) and show the loop retrying once, then stopping with a clear stop reason.
practice.done_when: `python agent.py --task ...` finishes 10 sample tasks; trace.jsonl has one line per step with step, tool, args, result/error, tokens; a test proves the loop stops at max_steps and on budget exhaustion.

quiz.prompt: Which stop condition prevents an infinite tool loop when the model never says 'done'?
quiz.explain: Only a hard bound guarantees termination.

quiz.prompt: An 'observation' in ReAct is…
options: the tool result fed back into context
quiz.explain: Act produces a tool call; the observation is its result appended for the next step.

quiz.prompt: Native reasoning models (2025–26) mainly change…
options: whether you prompt explicit 'Thought:' text; the act/observe loop stays
quiz.explain: Reasoning happens inside the model, but tool execution and observation remain your loop's job.

quiz.prompt: List your loop's stop reasons and say which one should page a human.
rubric: Lists ≥ 4 distinct stop reasons (done, max_steps, budget, tool_fatal, policy_denied…)
Picks one that signals an unsafe or unresolvable state
Justifies with impact (side effects, cost, user waiting)

creates a new ticket on every retry

quiz.prompt: Absolute file paths help agent tools because…

quiz.prompt: A good tool error message…

is a raw stack trace only

quiz.prompt: Plan-and-execute mainly reduces…
options: the number of model calls spent re-planning at each step

quiz.prompt: Reflexion stores…
options: verbal feedback from past attempts in memory

quiz.prompt: Comparing patterns fairly requires…

code can compose many operations and loops in one action

practice.title: Compaction at 70%
practice.brief: Add token accounting to your loop and a compaction step at 70% of budget that keeps the goal, decisions, open issues, tool-call ids and the raw observations of failed steps. Run a 30-step task with and without compaction.
practice.done_when: A report shows success with vs without compaction, tokens saved, and a list of facts that were lost (or 'none') checked by a test that asserts the goal and failed-step ids survive compaction.

quiz.prompt: 'Context rot' means…
options: performance drops as the context fills with irrelevant tokens
quiz.explain: More tokens ≠ better; attention is a finite budget.

quiz.prompt: A safe compaction keeps…
options: the goal, decisions, open issues and references to raw observations
quiz.explain: Compaction must keep what the next step needs plus pointers to evidence.

quiz.prompt: Just-in-time context means…
options: loading identifiers/handles and fetching contents when needed
quiz.explain: Keep lightweight references, pull details on demand.

quiz.prompt: Name one fact your agent must never lose in compaction, and explain how you'd enforce it.

Enforces it structurally (pinned state field, not left to the summariser)

quiz.prompt: Durable user memory differs from RAG over documents because…
options: it is written by the agent and needs provenance, correction and deletion
quiz.explain: Agent-written facts can be wrong and must be editable.

quiz.prompt: The risk of auto-writing memories from tool output is that…
options: injected or false facts persist across sessions
quiz.explain: Memory turns a one-off injection into a persistent one.

quiz.prompt: Episodic memory is best described as…
quiz.explain: Episodic = what happened; semantic = facts.

practice.title: Kill it mid-tool-call
practice.brief: Make your plain-Python agent resumable: persist state to SQLite after each step, kill the process mid-tool-call and resume. Add an approval interrupt before any write tool, and exponential backoff with jitter that does not retry non-idempotent writes without checking external state.
practice.done_when: A scripted test kills the process at a random step 5 times and every run resumes to completion with no duplicated write; the approval prompt blocks writes until approved.

quiz.prompt: After a crash during a non-idempotent payment tool, the safe action is to…
options: check the external system state/idempotency key before retrying
quiz.explain: You must know whether the side effect already happened.

quiz.prompt: A checkpoint should contain…
options: enough state to resume deterministically (messages, tool results, step counter, pending approvals)
quiz.explain: Resume needs the full decision state.

quiz.prompt: Exponential backoff with jitter prevents…
quiz.explain: Jitter spreads retries so clients don't hammer a recovering service together.

quiz.prompt: Which steps in your agent are safe to replay, and which aren't?
rubric: Classifies reads/pure computations as safe
Classifies writes/external side effects as unsafe unless idempotent
Describes how the checkpoint records completion of side effects

quiz.prompt: In MCP 2026-07-28, protocol version negotiation happens…
options: per request via _meta (plus an HTTP header on Streamable HTTP)
quiz.explain: The 2026-07-28 core is stateless; there is no initialize handshake.

quiz.prompt: MCP tools vs resources:
options: tools are model-invoked actions; resources are URI-addressed data
quiz.explain: Prompts are user-controlled templates; resources are read by URI.

quiz.prompt: Does MCP itself decide whether an action is authorized?
options: No — authorization stays with the host, credentials and your policy
quiz.explain: MCP is a transport/contract; policy is your job.

quiz.prompt: Why does a stateless protocol core make horizontal scaling and retries easier?
rubric: Any replica can serve any request (no session affinity)
Retries don't depend on server-held session state
Mentions that application state must then be explicit (ids/handles)

practice.title: Scoped tokens and a poisoned tool
practice.brief: Put your HTTP MCP server behind OAuth (local auth server or a free IdP tier — check current terms). Issue one read-scoped and one write-scoped token. Add a 'poisoned' third-party tool whose description hides instructions and show your host's allowlist + description-hash pinning blocks it.

quiz.prompt: Tool poisoning is…
options: malicious instructions hidden in tool descriptions/metadata that the model reads
quiz.explain: Descriptions enter the model's context, so they are an injection channel.

quiz.prompt: Forwarding the user's token unchanged to downstream APIs (token passthrough) is…
options: an anti-pattern — issue properly scoped tokens per audience
quiz.explain: Audience-bound tokens prevent confused-deputy attacks.

quiz.prompt: Pinning a tool's description hash protects against…
quiz.explain: A server can silently change a tool's description after you approved it.

quiz.prompt: Explain the difference between authenticating the client app and authorizing the user's action.
